messages.author: d34d025a513c07fc
messages.subject: ggplot2 performance poll
parts:
Hi everyone -

I'm trying to figure out why ggplot2 does stuff at very different speeds on different machines, and I was hoping you could help collect data.

Here's the background: I've been generating a lot of ggplot2 graphs recently on two different machines, and I've noticed big differences in performance, when, based on the hardware specs, there shouldn't be much of a difference.

One of the machines is a Macbook Air, Core i7 1.7Ghz. The other is a Dell desktop Core 2 Quad 2.3GHz, running Ubuntu Linux. They should take about the same amount of time to run the same code, since it's single-threaded, and the i7 should be faster per clock cycle. However the actual times I get for a particular graph are:
- Mac: 7.8 s
- Linux: 3.3 s
- Linux in VirtualBox VM on Mac: 7.3 s

I'm trying to figure out if the Mac hardware is just slow, or if something else is going on. I'd appreciate it if you could run the following code, then copy and paste the dput() results into the form linked to below:

library(ggplot2)  
p <- ggplot(diamonds, aes(clarity, carat)) + geom_boxplot() + facet_grid(. ~ cut)
pdf('temp.pdf')
time <- benchplot(p)
dev.off()
unlink('temp.pdf')  # Remove the temporary file

time  # Print time info

dput(list(ver = R.Version(), time = time))


https://docs.google.com/spreadsheet/viewform?formkey=dDd6b2Q5MG9ic2NoQWRPT3dLT0FyUkE6MQ

I don't know how to collect information about the CPU from within R, so the form also asks you to enter that information. (I don't know that much about the various kinds of CPUs, especially AMD hardware, so if there are any common CPU types that I'm missing, please let me know.)

Thanks!
-Winston

I tried to figure out possible causes. For those who wondered, an interactive execution and R CMD batch give approximately the same result so it's not something that would be better optimized on Linux on this end.

Given the description of the machines and the fact that you make us write a PDF in the test, I would have said that disk speed was the culprit but the MB Air has a solid state drive which should be faster than the probably regular disk in the Dell.

Good luck figuring out what happens.

JiHO

messages.author: d34d025a513c07fc
messages.subject: Re: ggplot2 performance poll
parts:
Oh, it's probably a good idea to use a fresh R session, the latest version of R (2.14.2) and definitely use ggplot2 0.9.0. This is a very unscientific poll with probably a very small sample size, so I'm not super concerned about making sure everything is controlled. If you have multiple machines running different operating systems, it would be great if you could test both.

What would really be helpful are tests on the same hardware running different operating systems. Maybe if I feel really ambitious I'll try to figure out how to boot my Mac into Linux and test that.

So far it looks like Macs are the most popular, with twice as many Macs as Windows and Linux machines!

-Winston

 x86_64 darwin9.8.0 Core i7     2  1.80      7.760      MacBook Air


Here's the script if you want to download and look at the data yourself:
 https://gist.github.com/2213801
There's a bit more information in the data set than what I showed above, including some reports of local weather conditions. :)

Anyway, it looks like maybe it's just that my computer is unusually slow -- it took about twice as long as the next slowest computer. I decided to run Geekbench on my computer, and it comes out at about 1/3 the speed of other computers that are the exact same model, even after a reinstall of the OS. So it seems likely that there's just something wrong with my computer, instead of something wrong with R or ggplot2 on Macs.

-Winston
